answer: Yes, that's expected. The current dispatcher passes only the first captured value to `run`. The workaround is to capture the whole suffix in one group, such as `lookup:(.+)`. Then split it inside the callback, for example with `suffix:match("([^:]+):(.+)")`. This is described in the "Multiple capture groups" section of `Virtual Pages.md`.

8	Virtual pages are read-only pages that don’t exist as files in your space. Instead, they are generated dynamically when you navigate to them. This is useful for building pages whose content is computed on-the-fly — for example, pages that show all objects with a particular tag.
9	
10	# How it works
11	You define a virtual page by calling `virtualPage.define` with a Lua pattern and a function. When someone navigates to a page name matching the pattern, SilverBullet calls your function instead of loading a file from disk.
12	
13	The current standard-library dispatcher passes the first captured value from the pattern to the function. The function returns the Markdown content to display. Put definitions in a `space-lua` block in your own space, then run `System: Reload`.
14	
15	```lua
16	virtualPage.define {
17	  pattern = "greeting:(.+)",
18	  run = function(name)
19	    return "# Hello, " .. name .. "!\nWelcome to this virtual page."
20	  end
21	}
22	```
23	
24	Navigating to `greeting:World` renders a page with the heading “Hello, World!” — but no file is created.
25	
26	Virtual pages are always **read-only**. The editor disables editing controls automatically.
27	
28	# Built-in virtual pages
29	## Tag pages
30	The most commonly used virtual pages are **tag pages**. When you click a hashtag like `#project`, SilverBullet navigates to `tag:project`, which is a virtual page that lists all objects with that tag — grouped by type (pages, tasks, items, data, etc.).
31	
32	Tag pages are defined in the standard library and work out of the box. You can override the default tag page by defining your own `virtualPage.define` with the pattern `tag:(.+)`.
33	
34	## URI pages
35	Navigating to a page named `uri:https://example.com/page` fetches and displays the content from that URL. This is useful for pulling in external markdown content.
36	
37	# Defining your own virtual pages
38	Here’s a more complete example that queries the object index:
39	
40	```lua
41	virtualPage.define {
42	  pattern = "recent:(%d+)",
43	  run = function(count)
44	    local n = tonumber(count)
45	    local pages = query[[
46	      from index.pages()
47	      order by lastModified desc
48	      limit n
49	    ]]
50	    local result = "# " .. count .. " Most Recent Pages\n"
51	    for _, page in ipairs(pages) do
52	      result = result .. "* " .. markdown.link(page.name) .. "\n"
53	    end
54	    return result
55	  end
56	}
57	```
58	
59	Navigate to `recent:10` to see the 10 most recently modified pages.
60	
61	# Multiple capture groups
62	The current dispatcher passes only the first match value to `run`. If you need several values, capture the complete suffix and parse it inside the callback:
63	
64	```lua
65	virtualPage.define {
66	  pattern = "lookup:(.+)",
67	  run = function(suffix)
68	    local kind, id = suffix:match("([^:]+):(.+)")
69	    if not kind then return "Use lookup:kind:id" end
70	    return "# " .. kind .. "\nLooking up: " .. id
71	  end
72	}
73	```
74	
75	# How it works under the hood
76	Virtual page definitions are stored in the config system under the `virtualPages` key. When a page is being created, SilverBullet fires the `editor:pageCreating` event. The standard library’s event listener checks all registered patterns against the page name. If a match is found, the corresponding `run` function is called, and its return value becomes the page content with read-only permissions.
77
